t9-mop: Bill Chen and Jerrod Ankenman's The Mathematics of Poker (2006) is the intellectual source of the solver era. Its methodology: rather than studying complex real poker directly, construct precisely solvable "toy games", and distill structural regularities that still hold in real hands. The bluff ratio b/(1+2b), MDF, and indifference principle you learned in T5 all originate from this line.
The [0,1] Game and the AKQ Game

One classic toy game is the AKQ game: the deck has only A, K, Q, each player gets one card in a single-street showdown. The equilibrium solution reveals three timeless roles: A (the nuts) always value-bets; Q (air) bluffs at a precise frequency; K (the medium hand) never bets — it can only be a bluff catcher, calling at an indifferent frequency. Every real hand at every node plays one of these three roles; this is the theoretical prototype of the "three-tier range structure" (value / medium / air).

AKQ equilibrium solution (fixed bet B, pot P; A always bets, Q bluffs at frequency f — defined as bluff combos ÷ value combos — and K calls at frequency c):
① Make K indifferent (call EV = fold EV = 0): the bluff share y of the betting range satisfies y×(P+B) = (1−y)×B → y = B/(P+2B), which as a bluff ÷ value ratio is f = y/(1−y) = B/(P+B)
② Make Q's bluff indifferent (bluff EV = check EV = 0): (1−c)×P = c×B → c = P/(P+B) — exactly the defender's MDF
③ Equilibrium: f = B/(P+B) and c = P/(P+B) — same denominator, numerators swapped, so f + c = 1: bluff frequency and call frequency are complements, not equals
Example: bet = pot (B=P) → f = 1/2, c = 1/2 (they coincide numerically at this one size only); betting 1/3 pot → f = 1/4, c = 3/4
This is the isomorphic source of MDF and Alpha in the minimal model (T5): f = Alpha = b/(1+b), c = MDF = 1/(1+b), while the bluff share inside the betting range follows its own formula y = b/(1+2b). (Concept from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.5 toy games and the AKQ equilibrium)

Example 2 (mapping AKQ to real hands): On the river you hold medium strength (the K role) and the opponent bets one pot. In equilibrium his bluff frequency f = 1/2, so you should call with K-type hands at c = 1/2 (with MDF, fully derived in T5). If the opponent is observed to never bluff (f far below 1/2), lower your call frequency accordingly — the toy game provides the baseline for adjustment; real hand reading provides the deviation direction.

Example 3 (the preflop version of the three roles): Preflop BTN opens, BB defends. BB's calling range against the open has three classes: strong hands (A role, continue 3-betting or slow-play), medium hands (K role, only call to showdown), bluff candidates (Q role, occasionally 3-bet-bluffing). MOP's three-tier structure is the skeleton of range construction — for every hand preflop you must first ask: "is this hand an A, K, or Q in this spot?"

The deepest conclusion of the AKQ game: the correct strategy for medium strength is passivity (check/call); betting belongs to the two poles. This conclusion cuts through every level — "betting medium hands" remains the most common amateur leak (T6 argued the same thing from a sizing angle).
The Stratification of Strategy and Tactics

MOP also establishes the levels of analysis: the tactical layer solves "how to play this hand", the strategic layer solves "how to construct my whole range". The book's famous insight: the weak think about single hands, the strong think about ranges, the strongest think about the rules of range construction. Modern solvers are the engineering of this idea: they never tell you "what to do with this hand" — they output the whole range's allocation over the game tree.

Example: MOP's risk-aversion theory also answers a practical question: when you have a significant technical edge, you can moderately avoid small +EV all-ins with high variance (preserving the opportunity to realize your edge); conversely, as the weaker side you should actively embrace variance. This gives a rigorous mathematical statement for "good players avoid big-coinflip pots with better players" — not just street wisdom.

The right way to read MOP: don't derive every page; grasp what variable each toy game isolates and what the conclusion is. Toy games are to poker what inclined-plane experiments are to physics — simplification isn't distortion, it's developing the image.
Self-test your depth: can you use the AKQ game to explain to a friend "why medium hands shouldn't bet" and "why bluffs must exist"? If you can explain both clearly, you've grasped MOP's essence.
t9-icm: In cash games, 1 chip is always = 1 unit of money. In tournaments it isn't: the prize ladder (e.g. 30% first, 20% second...) makes chip marginal value decrease — double your chips and your prize expectation is far from double; losing your chips costs all remaining expectation. ICM (Independent Chip Model) is the standard model converting "chip counts" into "prize expectation ($EV)": it recursively computes the probability of finishing each place by chip share, and weights the prizes for true value.

ICM's core corollary: an all-in that is "cEV-neutral or even slightly positive" in tournament chips can be significantly $EV-negative. Survival itself has value — this is the root of tournament strategy diverging from cash-game strategy.

ICM recursive algorithm (simplified 3-player SNG, prize 50/30/20, chips A=5000/B=3000/C=2000):
Step 1 (first-place probability = chip share): P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.3, P(C)=0.2
Step 2 (recursive second place): P(A 2nd) = P(B wins)×A/(A+C) + P(C wins)×A/(A+B) = 0.3×5000/7000 + 0.2×5000/8000 ≈ 0.339
P(B 2nd) = 0.5×3000/5000 + 0.2×3000/8000 = 0.375
P(C 2nd) = 0.5×2000/5000 + 0.3×2000/7000 ≈ 0.286
Step 3 (third = 1 minus the first two): P(A 3rd) ≈ 0.161, P(B 3rd) = 0.325, P(C 3rd) ≈ 0.514
Step 4 (weighted prizes): $EV(A) = 0.5×50 + 0.339×30 + 0.161×20 ≈ 38.4
$EV(B) = 0.3×50 + 0.375×30 + 0.325×20 ≈ 32.8
$EV(C) = 0.2×50 + 0.286×30 + 0.514×20 ≈ 28.9
Check: 38.4+32.8+28.9 ≈ 100 (prize conservation), and A's $EV share 38.4% < chip share 50% — decreasing marginal value visualized. (Concept from: ICM Theory independent-chip-model recursive definition)

Example 2 (the intuition of recursion): Step 2's recursion — "A finishes second" decomposes into "if B wins first, A competes with C for second" + "if C wins first, A competes with B for second". Each step asks "after removing the winner from the table, the rest compete by chips for the next place". Real ICM calculators repeat this recursion at higher dimensions (6-9 players), done by program when many players remain.

Example 3 (using the computed results): In the example above, A has 50% of the chips but is worth only 38.4% of the prize pool. To let this change a decision you need a spot where losing really does mean zero — that holds when a big stack shoves on a short stack, not the other way round (A=5000 shoving into B=3000 still leaves A with 2000 after losing, which is hardly zero). Take the medium stack M (3000) facing a shove from the big stack (5000): M is fully covered, so losing is elimination. Folding banks the already computed $EV(M) = 32.8. If M calls and wins (assume 55% equity) M moves to 6000 and the table becomes 6000/2000/2000; the recursion gives P(M 1st)=0.6, P(M 2nd)=0.2×6/8 + 0.2×6/8 = 0.3, P(M 3rd)=0.1, so $EV = 0.6×50 + 0.3×30 + 0.1×20 = 41.0. Calling therefore expects 0.55×41.0 + 0.45×0 = 22.6, below the 32.8 of folding — the quantified demo of "winning mathematically, folding on ICM": it's not that 55% is insufficient; it's that chips' marginal value is compressed by the tournament prize structure. Move the same hand to a cash table: risk 3000 to win 3000 at 55% and the expectation is +300 chips, an uncontested call. The two ledgers diverge because of the utility function, not because of nerve.

Example: On the bubble (one more elimination and everyone gets paid), you're medium-stacked and a big stack shoves on you. Even if you judge 55% equity (clearly +cEV), calling may still be a $EV disaster: winning adds limited chip value, losing zeroes 100% of your prize expectation; and the opponents the big stack can't eliminate are waiting for you two to collide. Conversely this is precisely the big stack's weapon — ICM pressure lets him push every medium stack with an extremely wide range: you "know he's stealing", yet mathematically you can only fold.

(1) The bubble and money-jump stages are the most distorted: medium stacks play tightest, big stacks most aggressively, and small stacks can play almost normally (they're about to be gone anyway); (2) push/fold charts in shallow stacks (<15bb) are almost entirely determined by ICM and math — memorizable away from the table; (3) the fair baseline for final-table deals is the ICM value — those who don't know ICM lose once at the negotiating table.

Know ICM's boundaries too: it ignores position, technical edge, and blinds rising (assumes equal skill and immediate settlement), so technically superior players may slightly deviate from ICM's conservative solutions (future edge still realizable), and it also undervalues the big stack's bullying value early in the FT. The model is a map, not the territory.

The most common ICM disaster isn't miscalculation but disregard: playing the bubble with cash-game intuition, "I have AJo, why should I fold" — because of the prize structure. Every tournament decision must run two books: one cEV, one $EV, and the latter governs.
Training order suggestion: first memorize the sub-15bb push/fold base charts, then review your own bubble decisions with an ICM calculator — these two are the highest-ROI homework for tournament ROI.

ICM conversion for a 3-player SNG (prizes 50/30/20, stacks 5000/3000/2000): the larger the stack share, the lower its $EV share — diminishing chip value is exactly where ICM pressure comes from. The three $EV figures sum to 100.
t9-multiway: Each additional opponent dilutes your showdown equity once: AA is about 85% heads-up but falls to ~64% four-way; for "ranges" it's crueler — heads-up top pair weak kicker is a good hand, but in a four-way pot it's often just a paying second place. The first law of multiway pots: the made-hand threshold rises across the board, and nuttiness trumps everything — hands that can make the nuts (suited connectors, pocket pairs) appreciate, while dominated hands (weak Ax, KJo class) crash.

Multiway showdown equity table (typical starting hands vs N random opponents):
AA: 1 opponent ≈85%｜2 ≈73%｜3 ≈64%｜4 ≈56%｜5 ≈49%
KK: 1 ≈82%｜2 ≈69%｜3 ≈59%｜4 ≈51%
AKs: 1 ≈67%｜2 ≈50%｜3 ≈40%
87s: 1 ≈41%｜2 ≈30%｜3 ≈24%
Pattern: each extra opponent drops equity about 8-12 percentage points; big pairs dilute slowest and suited connectors resist best — because the latter's value comes from nut potential rather than current made strength. (Concept from: Multiway Theory multiway equity allocation)

Example 2 (using the equity table): You open AA from UTG and three callers make it a 4-way pot. Per the table AA showdown equity is still about 64%, but note this is "showdown" equity — every time a street threatens a straight/flush/set from one caller, your "realizable equity" drops further. Conclusion: even AA in multiway pots should bet fast to build the pot and control variables, not slow-play and give free cards.

Example 3 (87s counterintuition): In the table, 87s heads-up is only 41% — looks weak, yet in 3-4-way pots it still holds about 30% — because its value comes entirely from making straights/flushes postflop. This is the quantitative support for "multiway rewards nut potential": weak Ax is 55% heads-up but may drop below 25% in a 4-way pot (dominated), while 87s decays much more gently.

Bluffs depreciate sharply in multiway pots: a bluff needs everyone to fold, and success drops exponentially with player count; plus each extra opponent is another chance someone has hit the board. Multiway fundamentals: cut bluff frequency sharply, while value bets get called more easily — "play value in multiway, play pressure heads-up".

The most important theoretical change (warned in T5): the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee only holds for two-player zero-sum games. In multiway games, even if everyone plays "equilibrium", two players' strategic interaction can objectively squeeze a third (without collusion); one player's error can also happen to hurt another rather than benefit. So there's no "copy-and-safe" GTO multiway — solid fundamentals (tight, value-oriented, position) and reads on specific opponents weigh far more than equilibrium dogma.

Example: BTN limps behind CO's open, and you're in the BB with A5s facing 2.5bb. Heads-up this is a standard 3-bet-bluff candidate (blocker + nut potential), but now you're squeezed in the middle: a 3-bet must get through two ranges at once, and once called your A5s can't continue on most flops in a 3-way 3-bet pot. Multiway dynamics turn a "beautiful equilibrium play" into lighting fireworks — the correct answer retreats to call or fold.

In multiway pots the "protection" value of betting rises (the more live hands, the more valuable making equity fold), and the cost of slow-playing rises too — giving three opponents free cards is giving three chances to outdraw. On defense, responsibility is shared: facing a bet, MDF doesn't need to be met by you alone; the player with the best position/hand structure takes more of the defense; in the sandwich spot (between the bettor and yet-to-act players), your calling range must be much tighter than heads-up.

Multiway discipline checklist: starting hands favor nut potential, bluff less postflop, fast-play strong hands instead of slow-playing, pot-control medium hands, and play tight in the sandwich position. Violating any one of these costs more than heads-up.

Low-stakes multiway pots are the profit home: opponents bring heads-up mindsets and play top pair weak kicker for all three streets in four-way pots. You need only one thing — be there with a nut-oriented range waiting for them.
t9-alpha:
Alpha = bet ÷ (pot + bet) — the break-even fold rate YOUR OWN bluff needs (an attacker-side number, not a threshold about how the opponent bluffs)

Example: when you bet 1/2 pot (bet=0.5pot)
- Alpha = 0.5/(1+0.5) = 33%
- The opponent's fold rate must exceed 33% for your bluff to profit

This is the "price tag" from the attacker's perspective, answering: "what minimum share of hands must the opponent fold for my bluff to break even?"

MDF and Alpha are the two sides of the same game tree, revealing the essence of game theory:
- MDF = pot/(pot+bet) — your defense frequency (defender's view)
- Alpha = bet/(pot+bet) — the fold rate the opponent needs (attacker's view)
- Key finding: MDF + Alpha = 1 (they are complements)

This duality shows that one side's optimal strategy exactly cancels the other side's exploitation space. The defender's MDF determines the attacker's Alpha, and vice versa. They share the same denominator (pot+bet) mathematically, differing only in numerator (pot vs bet).
Proof of MDF + Alpha = 1: pot/(pot+bet) + bet/(pot+bet) = (pot+bet)/(pot+bet) = 1

Alpha answers one attacker-side question: "does this bluff of mine break even?" —
- My bluff profits ⇔ the opponent's actual fold rate > Alpha
- It does not answer "should I call?" That is a defender-side question, settled by required equity = my call ÷ (pot + his bet + my call), which you then compare against your hand's equity versus his range (derivation in t5-mdf-alpha).

Three practical steps: 1) compute Alpha for the size you intend to use; 2) estimate his real fold rate on that street from stats (fold-to-c-bet, fold-to-big-river-bet and the like); 3) fold rate above Alpha ⇒ bluffing this size profits automatically, no showdown value required; below Alpha ⇒ this size burns money consistently.

Example 1: You bet 1/3 pot, Alpha = (1/3)÷(1+1/3) = 1/4 = 25%. His actual fold rate on this street is 30%, above 25% ⇒ your bluff profits. Recompute (pot = 1, bet = 1/3): EV = 0.30×1 − 0.70×(1/3) = +0.067, i.e. every bluff wins 6.7% of a pot on average; if he really folds only 20%, the same bluff becomes 0.20 − 0.80×(1/3) = −0.067.

Example 2: You bet 1/2 pot, Alpha = 0.5÷1.5 = 1/3 ≈ 33%. His fold rate is only 25%, below 33% ⇒ bluffing this size loses: EV = 0.25×1 − 0.75×0.5 = −0.125 (12.5% of a pot per bluff). The fix is to bluff less often (only bet when you still carry showdown value or improvement equity) or to size down — note Alpha climbs monotonically with size (1/4 pot 20%, 1/3 pot 25%, half pot 33%, pot 50%), so betting bigger only lifts the break-even hurdle higher; a larger size becomes an exploit once you have confirmed his fold rate rises faster than Alpha does.

Example 3: You bet 1/4 pot, Alpha = 0.25÷1.25 = 1/5 = 20%. His fold rate is exactly 20%, equal to Alpha ⇒ pure break-even, EV = 0: 0.20×1 − 0.80×0.25 = 0. Don't mistake this size for "a free bet that cannot lose" — it earns nothing at all; yet any fold rate above 20% makes it automatically profitable, which is precisely why balanced strategies pack so many bluffs into small, frequent sizes: the lowest break-even hurdle.

Alpha's application principle: quantitative comparison, not intuition. But what it measures is "how many folds my bluff at this size needs to break even", not "does he bluff enough for me to call" — reading an attacker-side metric as a defend-or-fold rule is the most common way this concept gets used backwards.

Self-test your depth: can you use Alpha to explain to a friend "why the very same 1/3-pot bet is a money printer against an opponent who folds 30% and a bonfire against one who folds 20%", and why "should I call?" requires a different formula? If you can cover both, you've grasped Alpha's essence.
t9-unified: The End of the False Dichotomy

"GTO camp vs exploitation camp" is a false dichotomy of the learning stage. In the complete framework both are two modes of one system: equilibrium is optimal without information (bulletproof vest against unknown opponents / strong players / insufficient samples), exploitation is optimal with information (harvest knife when leaks are confirmed). Every decision answers the same question: what my knowledge of the opponent supports — how much deviation, in what direction?

Decision = equilibrium baseline + f(information quality) × directed deviation
Zero information → pure baseline; complete information and non-adapting opponent → maximal exploitation; in between → scale deviation by confidence (concept from: Applications of NLHE equilibrium-exploitation unified framework)
The Knowledge Map Across Nine Levels

Looking back: T1-T2 gave you the measuring system (probability, EV, odds) — the units of all judgment; T3-T4 gave you the coordinate system (position, range) — where you are and what you fight against; T5-T6 gave you the equilibrium baseline (GTO, MDF, sizing theory) — the correct shape without information; T7 gave you the information system (stats, types, hand reading, exploitation) — turning observations into deviation evidence; T8 gave you operational safeguards (psychology, bankroll, state) — keeping the system stable on a real human; T9 assembles everything and annotates each tool's applicability boundary (multiway, ICM, model limits).

The framework's operating loop: start from the equilibrium baseline → accumulate information through observation → deviate with evidence (exploitation) → monitor opponent adaptation → retreat or counter → escorted throughout by psychology and bankroll systems. This loop has no endpoint — poker is never "finished", only versioned.

Example: One river full-pot bet decision, all nine levels show up — pot odds says you need 33% equity (T2); range filtering + combo counting says he bluffs about 25% (T4/T7); equilibrium says "should" be 33% bluffs here (T5); his WTSD and river AF say this player never bluffs big on the river (T7); you just lost a big pot, and the checklist reminds you not to comfort yourself with "he always bluffs" (T8) — fold. A decision's quality equals the number of theories correctly invoked behind it.

Example 2 (confidence-driven deviation): You collect 200 hands and find an opponent folds to C-Bets 65% (far above equilibrium ~45%) — high confidence. Your deviation: raise C-Bet frequency and bluff share, specifically firing at him. But if the sample is only 15 hands, 65% may be noise — at low confidence, return to baseline. Same observation, two different-magnitude decisions; the difference is entirely information quality.

Example 3 (the adaptation-monitoring loop): Three times in a row you fold bluff catches using the read "he never bluffs big on the river". The fourth time he shoves, you fold, and he shows pure air — an adaptation signal. This isn't discarding the read but downgrading it to "usually true", returning to the equilibrium baseline while waiting for new samples. Exploitation is a dynamic game: you adjust others, and others adjust you.

Suggested reading order: The Theory of Poker (Sklansky, intellectual awakening) → The Mental Game of Poker (Tendler, psychological system) → Applications of No-Limit Hold'em (Janda, equilibrium application) → Modern Poker Theory (Acevedo, solver-era synthesis) → The Mathematics of Poker (Chen & Ankenman, mathematical foundation). Toolchain: solver + database + this platform's training modules — theory closes the loop into muscle memory here.

The final warning is the same as the first principle: theory has value only when executed. Knowing MDF yet over-folding under pressure, understanding variance yet tilting after a Bad Beat — the gap between knowing and doing is the distance between you and your ceiling.

Graduation assignment: after finishing this level, go to the Strategy Academy and training modules to practice each theory at least once (range training → T3/T4, odds quizzes → T1/T2, GTO simulator → T5/T6). The Theory Academy gives you the map; the training ground lets you walk the path.
t9-cash-vs-mtt: Two Ledgers for the Same Hand

Cash and tournaments are usually described as the same game played two ways. What actually differs is three things: the mapping from chips to money, the way the structure moves through time, and the form in which the house takes its cut. Those three are enough to make the same hand produce opposite answers. This chapter does not ask which format pays more - that needs a common unit first - it lays the two decision ledgers side by side so you always know which one you are computing in.

The comparison needs only six axes: effective depth (constant vs one-way collapse), chip utility (linear vs non-linear), form of the take (per pot vs per entry), player pool (drifts fast vs errors that stay put), time structure (blind levels that never change vs levels that always change) and variance shape (per-pot swings vs results concentrated in the finish). Switching axis by axis explains a profit gap better than "which format I am used to".
The Anchor: One Hand, Two Conclusions

Keep the same table already recomputed in the ICM chapter of this level: prizes 50/30/20, stacks 5000/3000/2000. The medium stack M = 3000 faces a shove from the big stack of 5000 and you judge 55% equity.
Cash: risk 3000 to win 3000, expectation = 0.55×3000 − 0.45×3000 = +300 chips, so call.
Tournament: M is fully covered, losing means out. Folding keeps a computed $EV of 32.8; calling and winning leaves 6000/2000/2000 whose recursion gives $EV = 41.0, so the expectation is 0.55×41.0 + 0.45×0 = 22.6 < 32.8, so fold.
The same 55% produces opposite instructions in the two ledgers.

Example 1 (why they disagree): in cash the 3001st chip is worth exactly the first chip, so any equity above 50% makes a fifty-fifty gamble worthwhile. In a tournament that is not true - after folding, M still holds a certain 32.8, and calling trades that 32.8 for a shot at 41.0, which is only about 25% more, not enough to pay for a 45% chance of zero. The disagreement comes from whether the chips-to-money curve is a straight line, not from nerve or skill. This is exactly where the ICM chapter said the model is a map and not the territory: change the map and the same mountain has a different height.
Is Depth Constant, or Does It Flow One Way

In cash the effective depth is a constant: you sit down with 100 big blinds and you stay near 100 big blinds all night. In a tournament M = effective stack ÷ big blind is an independent variable that moves in one direction only: blind levels rise on a clock while stacks do not grow by themselves. A stack of 10,000 is M = 50 at 100/200 and only M = 10 at 500/1000 - the same chips, a few levels later, are a different game. The real consequence of a collapsing M is not simply "play tighter": it deletes the sizing family. Below about 15bb the three postflop streets compress into a single shove and Push/Fold charts take over the decision (see the ICM chapter), while the check-raises, three-barrel fire and geometric sizings you drilled at 100bb simply do not exist in that M band.

Example 2 (one hand, two fates): A♠5♦ in a 100bb cash game is a speculative hand worth opening with position, with many streets left to realise equity; the same card at tournament M = 8 has only two actions available, and the test becomes "does its all-in equity clear the Push threshold for this position" rather than "how much equity can I realise postflop". The hand did not get worse - the mechanism by which it earns (implied equity) was removed by the structure. Symmetrically, a player who only ever practised 100bb cash will bleed at M = 8, because the postflop he is waiting for never arrives.
Rake and Tournament Fee: Same Name, Different Mechanism

Cash: net μ = gross μ − the amount taken per 100 hands. Rake is charged as a percentage of each pot (see T4, The Economics of Table Structure), so it punishes volume - every pot pays.
Tournament: net $EV per entry = $EV per entry − the fee. The fee is charged once per buy-in, independently of how many pots you play, so it punishes entries.
To compare them, write both over the same denominator: convert the cash result into per hour per buy-in, and spread the fee over hours. Both then answer the same question - how much does one hour of skilled play cost in toll.

Example 3 (the illusion of a fixed percentage): a fee of $10+$1 is 10% of the buy-in, $500+$20 is 4%, $2,000+$100 is 5% (indicative magnitudes only; structures differ by site). This explains two things that cause each other: the lowest buy-ins tax skill the hardest, and precisely for that reason their pools are the softest. A heavy-rake cash game (about 5bb/100, indicative) cannot be dodged by paying a smaller fee at all, because rake follows pots - the only hedges are fewer marginal participations and changing tables. The same sentence "this game is hard to beat" points at two different actions in the two structures: change table, or change buy-in.

Pools and drift also come in two forms (this is where the metagame drift of T7 lands). A cash pool is a continuous market: the same regulars sit across from you all month, exploitation conclusions have a short shelf life because opponents adapt within the session, and the remedy is constant re-measurement. A low-stakes tournament pool is a recurring novice market: the structural errors are extremely stable (ignoring the blind clock, folding too much at the bubble, and the opposite version of refusing to fold), but each tournament lasts a few hours, so the goal is not to teach an opponent on the spot - it is to repeat the same exploitation over a thousand entries. The first is a depreciable asset, the second an amortisable one; the amortisation period is long, which is why tournament exploitation knowledge is actually the more durable of the two.

The classic mistake: "Which one pays more - just look at the buy-ins and the profit figures." The two profit streams are not in the same unit. Cash is bb/100 × hands, with linear utility and a withdrawable balance; a tournament is a per-entry $EV distribution, concentrated at the top and needing tens to hundreds of entries to converge. Comparing the amounts directly is comparing kilometres with kilograms. The workable version converts both to the same time unit (per hour) and the same risk yardstick (risk adjusted), and only then asks which is larger.

A transfer-training order: drill the decision tree in cash first - unlimited re-entry, stable depth, feedback you can verify on the spot; then train the two tournament-only skills separately, Push/Fold charts below 15bb and bubble ICM judgement, reviewed off-line with a calculator rather than by feel at the table. Finally bring one habit across: check the structure before you sit. Rake at this table, fee at that event, and how often the blinds move - three tables are three different equations.

Two structures, two ledgers: the cash ledger counts hands and μ under linear utility, the tournament ledger counts $EV under non-linear utility with an M that collapses one way. The same 55% hand is a call worth +300 chips on one side and 22.6 against 32.8, a fold, on the other. The split does not come from skill but from which ledger you are computing in - so confirm the ledger before every decision.
t9-sixmax-capstone: Compressing Nine Levels Into One Decision Chain

By the end of the theory, every decision at the table breaks into five steps: read your position and effective stack, assign the opponent a range, judge whose range the board belongs to, read what his line on each street removes from that range, and only then decide whether to deviate from equilibrium for an exploit. The order cannot be reversed — deciding to exploit before defining ranges means picking evidence for a conclusion, and your review will never find the step where it went wrong. The cash-versus-tournament split lands on the first step too: the same chip count carries a different risk weight in the two formats, so the hands you can commit differ.

The five-step decision chain
1) Position and effective stack → compute the SPR and decide how many chips this hand is willing to fight for
2) Opponent range → derive width and strength distribution from his raise and call frequencies and from his position
3) Board → who holds more top pair or better, and who holds more nutted combos
4) Line → what each check, bet and call removes from his range on each street
5) Exploit → which direction to deviate and by how much
How you are scored: if the first four steps are wrong, an elegant fifth step is still wrong
One Hand Through All Five Steps

Steps one and two (6-max, 100bb, no ante): the hero opens to 2.5bb from the hijack with A♣Q♥, the button calls and both blinds fold. Pot = 0.5 + 1.0 + 2.5 + 2.5 = 6.5bb, each player has put in 2.5, the effective remaining stack is 97.5bb and SPR = 97.5 ÷ 6.5 = 15.0 — deep enough that a single pair should not be playing for stacks. The read on the opponent: VPIP 32 / PFR 10 / AF 1.0, an opening range on the strong side with almost no postflop raises and almost no bluffs. His flatting range therefore leans to medium pairs, suited connectors and dominated broadways like KQ and AJ, while AA, KK and AK would have raised preflop and are not in it.

Step three (the board): the flop comes Q♦8♣4♣. The hero holds top pair, top kicker, and the A♣ adds both a backdoor nut flush and a blocker — the opponent cannot hold an A♣-led flush draw. On this board QQ, 88 and AQ are denser in the raiser’s range, while 44, 9♣8♣ and 7♣6♣ sit in the button’s flatting range. With 6.5bb in the pot the hero bets 2bb (about 31%); one reason for the small size is position, since the hijack is out of position against the button and a big bet would collapse his range into two poles. The button calls and the pot becomes 10.5bb. The key information from that line is that he did not raise: sets, two pair and strong draws are all trapped inside a call, so his range is capped.

Step four (the line): the turn is 9♣. It completes both the flush and the T-J straight, and the hero holds only the A♣ of clubs. The hero checks, the button bets 6bb into 10.5bb (about 57%). The equity needed to call is 6 ÷ (10.5 + 6 + 6) = 6 ÷ 22.5 ≈ 26.7%; the hero has 9 flush cards plus the one remaining queen (the other queen is a club already counted), 10 ÷ 46 ≈ 22% of improvement, plus the times the opponent bets something worse, so the threshold is reachable and he calls. The pot is 22.5bb with 89.5bb behind. What carries the most information here is his bet rather than the hero’s cards: a player with an aggression factor of 1.0 who bets the turn voluntarily is usually already ahead of top pair.

Step five (exploit and close out): the river is 5♦ and every draw has missed. The hero checks, the button bets 15bb into 22.5bb (about 67%). The equity needed to call is 15 ÷ (22.5 + 15 + 15) = 15 ÷ 52.5 ≈ 28.6%, and the hero folds. The reason is not that top pair is small, it is the range: this board completed every draw, so the value combos that a player who never bluffs can represent across three streets (flushes, sets, straights) far outweigh the bluff combos he might hold; and because the A♣ has been in the hero’s hand the whole time, the opponent cannot even hold the strongest flush draw. Meeting an equity threshold does not force a call — reading the range can turn a call that the pot odds justify into a fold.
The Leak Checklist and Pool Exploits

A checklist only works when each item lands on a specific street: did you pick hands preflop because you wanted to play rather than because they were worth playing; when the board got wet did you keep using your flop sizing and treat medium strength as strength; out of position did you chase weak draws as if they were strong ones; on the river did you call because the pot odds said so without counting how many bluff combos he could still hold; and how often did the same mistake appear inside one session. Track frequency rather than money, because money is mixed with variance while frequency is a technical problem you can fix.

Pool exploits are graded by the opponent’s inverse leak. Against a player who calls too much: increase the size of value bets and cut bluffs to nearly zero, because he does not supply the fold rate a bluff needs. Against a player who folds too much and rarely raises: shrink value sizes and bluff more, since his fold rate sits far above the threshold. Against a chronic over-folder: use more small bets to collect rent and turn every street’s fold into profit. Against an over-aggressive player: bluff less and convert medium strength into bluff-catchers so his frequencies pay you. Every adjustment rests on the first four steps being right — with the range misread, an exploit just doubles the size of the mistake.

Long-term profit comes from executing the same decision chain again and again, not from the occasional brilliant fold. Fix the process so that every step can be reviewed, then let the checklist surface the one class of mistake that keeps repeating — that changes results more than memorising any range chart.

The five-step decision chain for 6-max cash: start from position and stack depth, move through opponent range and board ownership, then land on this street's goal and exploitative adjustment. Skip any step and every later conclusion loses its basis.

t9-mop-q1.question: MOP's core methodology is:
options: Statistical analysis of massive real hands
Constructing precisely solvable toy games and distilling general structural rules
t9-mop-q1.explanation: Real poker is too complex to solve directly; the precise solutions of simplified games reveal structures (bluff ratios, MDF, indifference) that still hold in real hands.

t9-mop-q2.question: In the AKQ game, K (the medium hand) 's equilibrium strategy is:
options: Never bet — only call as a bluff catcher at the right frequency
t9-mop-q2.explanation: K loses both ways if it bets (A always calls, Q always folds); its only value is catching Q's bluffs. This is the theoretical prototype of "medium strength should be passive".

t9-mop-q3.question: "The weak think about single hands, the strong think about ranges" reflects the stratification of:
options: The tactical layer (this hand) and the strategic layer (whole range construction)
t9-mop-q3.explanation: A single hand's optimal action can only be determined inside range-construction rules — solvers output range-level strategy, not single-hand answers.

t9-mop-q4.question: Per MOP's risk-aversion theory, a technically superior side should:
options: Moderately avoid small +EV spots with high variance, preserving room to realize the technical edge
t9-mop-q4.explanation: The superior side's edge produces EV every hour, so bearing huge variance for tiny immediate EV isn't worth it; the weaker side's logic is reversed and should actively raise variance.

t9-mop-q5.question: In the AKQ game, K (the medium hand) facing a 1-pot bet calls at an equilibrium frequency of:
t9-mop-q5.explanation: The defender's call frequency is c = P/(P+B): with B=P, c = P/(P+P) = 1/2. It shares the denominator with the bluff frequency f = B/(P+B) with the numerators swapped, so f + c = 1 — the toy-model prototype of the MDF/Alpha complementarity (at 1/3 pot they are 3/4 and 1/4, not equal).

t9-icm-q1.question: The core problem ICM solves is:
options: Converting tournament chip counts into true prize expectation ($EV)
t9-icm-q1.explanation: The prize ladder makes chip utility nonlinear; ICM computes each-place probabilities by chip share and weights the prizes to get chips' true monetary value.

t9-icm-q2.question: A "+cEV but −$EV" situation means:
options: Chip expectation rises but prize expectation falls — survival itself has value in tournaments
t9-icm-q2.explanation: Decreasing chip marginal value plus losing all expectation on bust makes chip-slightly-positive gambles negative in prize terms. Tournaments run on $EV.

t9-icm-q3.question: Under bubble ICM pressure, the typical behavior by stack size is:
options: Medium stacks tightest, big stacks most aggressive, small stacks near normal
t9-icm-q3.explanation: Medium stacks lose the most prize expectation so are the most suppressed; big stacks bully through this; small stacks have little remaining expectation and the least constraint.

t9-icm-q4.question: The correct understanding of ICM's model boundaries is:
options: ICM is perfect and must be strictly followed
It ignores position, skill edge, and blinds rising — technically superior players may deviate moderately from its conservative solutions
ICM only applies to cash games
ICM can't be used at final tables
t9-icm-q4.explanation: ICM assumes equal skill and immediate settlement. With a clear technical edge, future value supports leaning beyond survival/conservative choices. The model is a map, not the territory.

t9-icm-q5.question: 3-player SNG (prize 50/30/20), chips A=5000/B=3000/C=2000. A's $EV is about:
t9-icm-q5.explanation: P(A 1st)=0.5, 2nd≈0.339, 3rd≈0.161; $EV = 0.5×50+0.339×30+0.161×20 ≈ 38.4. Note it's well below the 50 his chip share implies — the visible face of decreasing chip marginal value. "50" reads the chip share as the prize share (cash-table thinking); "28.9" is C's $EV, i.e. the wrong player; "22.6" is the post-call expectation of the medium stack in Example 3, not the value A holds right now.

t9-multiway-q1.question: The pattern of starting-hand value changes in multiway pots is:
options: Hands that can make the nuts appreciate; easily dominated hands crash
t9-multiway-q1.explanation: Equity dilution raises the made-hand threshold: suited connectors/pocket pairs (nut potential) relatively appreciate, while weak Ax/KJo (often second place) crash.

t9-multiway-q2.question: Bluff frequency in multiway pots should:
options: Rise, because the pot is bigger
Drop sharply, because everyone must fold and success drops with player count
t9-multiway-q2.explanation: Bluff success ≈ the product of each opponent's fold rate, decaying exponentially with player count; and more players means more chance someone has hit the board.

t9-multiway-q3.question: The correct understanding of GTO in multiway pots is:
options: The unexploitable guarantee fails; fundamentals and opponent reads weigh more
Multiway pots have no theory at all
t9-multiway-q3.explanation: The Nash floor only holds for two-player zero-sum games; multiway dynamics can hurt even "equilibrium" players. Tight, value-oriented play and position are more reliable anchors.

t9-multiway-q4.question: The problem with slow-playing strong hands in multiway pots is:
options: No problem — more players means more reason to trap
Giving multiple opponents free cards equals giving multiple outdraw chances, and protection value is rising
Slow-playing is only a problem heads-up
t9-multiway-q4.explanation: The more live opponents, the higher the cumulative free-card outdraw probability and the greater the value of making equity pay — fast-play strong hands to build the pot multiway.

t9-multiway-q5.question: AA's showdown equity against 4 random opponents is about:
t9-multiway-q5.explanation: AA: 1 opponent ≈85%, 2 ≈73%, 3 ≈64%, 4 ≈56%. Each extra opponent drops about 8-12 points, and realizable equity is even lower — the mathematical basis for fast-playing strong hands and valuing nuttiness multiway.

t9-alpha-q1.question: What is Alpha's formula?
t9-alpha-q1.explanation: Alpha = bet / (pot + bet) = b/(1+b): the same denominator as MDF, with the numerator swapped for your own bet size, and the meaning "how often the opponent must fold for my bluff to break even". Option 0 is MDF; the two formulas dividing by a denominator containing 2×bet belong to the defender's "equity needed to call" (call ÷ (pot + his bet + my call)) — a different question from Alpha.

t9-alpha-q2.question: The relationship between Alpha and MDF is:
options: Alpha = MDF — two names for the same number
Alpha and MDF are reciprocals (Alpha × MDF = 1)
They are unrelated and computed independently
t9-alpha-q2.explanation: MDF = pot/(pot+bet) and Alpha = bet/(pot+bet): same denominator, and their two numerators add back up to that denominator, so Alpha + MDF = 1 (equivalently Alpha = 1 − MDF). They are not the same number (they only meet at 50% when b=1, a pot-size bet), not reciprocals, and not independent — both are fixed by the same bet size, and one side's optimal frequency exactly cancels the other side's exploitation room.

t9-alpha-q3.question: Alpha's core value lies in:
t9-alpha-q3.explanation: Alpha turns "how often must the opponent fold for this size of bluff to break even" into a numeric bar you can compare directly against his stats (1/3 pot → 25%, half pot → 33%, pot-size → 50%), which is what makes any deliberate deviation measurable; a qualitative view, a rule of thumb or intuition offers no checkable boundary. Note it serves the attacker's bluff decision, not "is he bluffing enough that I should call" — that second question uses the defender's required-equity formula.

t9-alpha-q4.question: Alpha's application steps are:
options: Compute Alpha → observe opponent fold rate → compare Alpha with his fold rate
Observe fold rate → compute Alpha → compare Alpha with his fold rate
Compare Alpha with fold rate → compute Alpha → observe fold rate
Observe fold rate → compare Alpha with fold rate → compute Alpha
t9-alpha-q4.explanation: The starting point can only be "which size am I going to use": Alpha is entirely determined by your own bet size (b/(1+b)), so without a size there is no Alpha and no bar to compare against; then you take his actual fold rate on that street, and finally compare — only a fold rate above Alpha makes the bluff profitable. The other three put observation or comparison before the calculation, i.e. reading data without a baseline, which cannot answer "does bluffing this size break even".

t9-alpha-q5.question: You plan to bluff 1/3 pot (Alpha = 1/4 = 25%), and your stats show the opponent folds 30% on this street. The conclusion is:
options: This size of bluff does not break even — stop using it
This size of bluff breaks even and profits, EV ≈ +0.067 pot
Size up to a pot-size bet instead — the bigger the bluff, the more it earns
Switch to MDF and decide whether to call
t9-alpha-q5.explanation: Fold rate 30% > Alpha 25% ⇒ EV = 0.30×1 − 0.70×(1/3) ≈ +0.067 pot, so this bluff profits without needing any showdown value (the same arithmetic as Example 1 in the chapter). "Does not break even" compares the two numbers backwards; "size up to pot" points the wrong way — a pot-size bet needs Alpha = 50%, so unless his fold rate rises faster than that, the same bluff becomes a steady loss; MDF and required equity handle the defender's calling question and say nothing about whether this bluff breaks even.

t9-unified-q1.question: The relationship between GTO and exploitation in the unified framework is:
options: Two modes of one system: equilibrium as the floor without information, exploitation by confidence with information
t9-unified-q1.explanation: Decision = equilibrium baseline + directed deviation weighted by information quality. Zero information → pure baseline; complete information → maximal exploitation; in between → scaled by confidence.

t9-unified-q2.question: The magnitude of deviating from equilibrium to exploit should depend on:
options: The information quality of the leak (sample and confidence) and the opponent's adaptation ability
t9-unified-q2.explanation: Deviations are justified by confirmed leaks; their upper bound is the opponent's counter-attack ability. Together they set the direction and magnitude of exploitation.

t9-unified-q3.question: The operating loop of the complete decision framework is:
options: Equilibrium baseline → observe → deviate with evidence → monitor adaptation → retreat/counter
t9-unified-q3.explanation: This loop integrates T5's equilibrium, T7's information and exploitation, and the adaptation arms race — executed with the psychological system's support from T8.

t9-unified-q4.question: The ultimate test of theoretical learning is:
options: How many formulas you can recite
Whether it changed real in-game decisions and can be executed steadily
t9-unified-q4.explanation: The knowing-doing gap is your skill ceiling. Theory must be converted through training into decision habits that survive pressure — exactly the closed loop between the Theory Academy and training modules.

t9-unified-q5.question: You collect 200 hands showing an opponent folds to C-Bets 65%, and start raising your bluff frequency against him. The basis of this deviation is:
options: An observable bias with sufficiently high confidence, the magnitude supported by information quality
t9-unified-q5.explanation: The unified framework requires deviations to be justified: sufficient sample (200 hands), a clear bias direction (folds too much), and continuous adaptation monitoring. Information quality sets deviation magnitude — the unified expression of GTO and exploitation.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q1.question: The medium stack of 3000 faces a shove from the 5000 big stack with 55% equity (prizes 50/30/20, short stack 2000). What are the correct cash and tournament conclusions?
options: Call in both, since 55% is ahead
Call in cash (expectation +300 chips), fold in the tournament (call 22.6 vs fold 32.8)
Fold in cash (too risky), call in the tournament (more chips means more aggression)
Fold in both, because the tournament conclusion should be carried back into cash
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q1.explanation: Cash risks 3000 to win 3000: 0.55×3000 − 0.45×3000 = +300 chips, so call. In the tournament M is fully covered: folding holds 32.8 while calling expects 0.55×41.0 = 22.6, so fold. Option 1 assumes 55% means the same thing in both ledgers, which is exactly the point at issue; option 3 inverts risk and depth (the covered short side is the one that must refuse); option 4 force-unifies the two ledgers, treating a non-linear-utility conclusion as portable into a linear one.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q2.question: A 10,000 stack goes from blinds 100/200 to 500/1000, so M falls from 50 to 10. The most direct consequence is:
options: Only the number changes; the shape of the strategy stays the same
Start making more small continuation bets
More streets of firing become available because the pots are relatively bigger
The sizing family collapses: below about 15bb the decision is taken over by shove-or-fold
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q2.explanation: M = effective stack ÷ big blind, so falling from 50 to 10 removes almost every postflop betting branch and the decision degenerates into shove or fold. Option 1 denies that depth determines strategy shape; option 2 reads shallower stacks as "slow play small bets", but small-bet branches need stack depth to be paid off; option 3 inverts SPR - with shallower stacks there is less room for multi-street firing and geometric sizings, not more.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q3.question: Which statement about cash rake and tournament fees is correct?
options: Rake is charged per pot and punishes volume; the fee is charged per entry and punishes entries
They are equivalent: both just take money from winnings
The fee is charged per pot, so the longer you play the more you pay
Rake exists only at micro stakes; regular levels have none
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q3.explanation: The difference is the mechanism, not the size: rake accrues with every pot, so calling more pots costs more, while the fee is fixed the moment you buy in and is independent of pots played. Option 2 erases that mechanism and with it the two different countermeasures - fewer marginal participations versus fewer entries. Option 3 swaps the two. Option 4 is false: rake exists at all levels, only the percentage and the cap differ.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q4.question: What does the difference between a $10+$1 fee (10%) and a $500+$20 fee (4%) tell you?
options: Higher buy-in games always have softer fields
Low buy-ins cost more in fees, so no profit is possible there
At the low end the fixed fee is a larger share of the buy-in, so the same skill edge is taxed away in a larger proportion
The percentage does not matter, only the absolute amount
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q4.explanation: The fee is a percentage of the buy-in and that percentage is highest at the low end, so an identical edge loses a tenth of itself at $10+$1 but only a twentieth at $500+$20. Option 2 overshoots - low buy-ins also have softer fields, and net profit depends on both. Option 1 equates high buy-ins with soft fields, which usually runs the other way (higher stakes are harder). Option 4 abandons the common denominator: two different sized games cannot be compared by absolute fee.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q5.question: To compare "do I make more from cash or from tournaments", the method must:
options: Compare total buy-ins against total winnings over the same period and pick the higher ratio
Convert both to the same time unit and the same risk yardstick, after subtracting each format’s own form of the take
Compare the single biggest cash hour against the single biggest tournament score
Look at which format has the higher ITM rate, since that is the profitable one
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q5.explanation: Cash is measured in bb/100 × hands with linear utility; a tournament is a per-entry $EV distribution, top-heavy and slow to converge. The only comparable form is same time unit, same risk adjustment, each net of its own mechanism of the take. Option 2 divides two non-comparable distributions; option 3 substitutes an extreme value for an expectation, which simply rewards whichever format has more variance; option 4 mistakes frequent cashing for profit, while a high ITM rate usually means the pay jumps are small.

t9-sixmax-capstone-q1.question: Which step comes first in the five-step decision chain?
options: Confirm position and effective stack, then compute the stack-to-pot ratio
Guess the two cards the opponent most likely holds
Decide the sizing for this street
Decide whether to bluff with this hand
t9-sixmax-capstone-q1.explanation: Position and effective stack set the parameters for every later step: the stack-to-pot ratio fixes the commitment line, and position fixes equity realisation and action order. Skipping it to guess hands or pick a size means computing inside the wrong coordinate system. Guessing hands and choosing bluffs are outputs of the fourth and fifth steps, and sizing follows from the structure of the range.

t9-sixmax-capstone-q2.question: Why can the same hand produce different conclusions in cash games and in tournaments?
options: Chips carry a different risk weight, so the same chip count represents a different value
Cash game decks are more likely to make a flush
Tournament blind structures do not allow all-in bets
Cash game opponents always have wider ranges
t9-sixmax-capstone-q2.explanation: Tournament chips have non-linear value: losing the whole stack costs far more than winning the same amount, so a higher equity is needed before committing. Cash game chips are close to fungible, so the criterion returns to pure expected value. Decks and all-in rules are identical in both formats, and opponent range width is not determined by the format itself.

t9-sixmax-capstone-q3.question: Against an opponent who calls too much and rarely folds, which way does the exploit point?
options: Increase value bet sizing and cut bluffs to nearly zero
Bluff more often and make him pay for being loose
Shrink value sizes to induce more raises
Raise your opening frequency to widen your range advantage
t9-sixmax-capstone-q3.explanation: A bluff needs the fold rate α = B/(P+B), which a calling station cannot supply, so any bluff is negative expectation; on the other side he will call wider sizes, so value bets can grow. The second option reverses the direction and is the adjustment for an over-folder; the third and fourth do not address the specific trait of not folding at all.

t9-mop-q6.question: In the AKQ toy game, the medium hand K's equilibrium strategy is:
t9-mop-q6.explanation: K beats only Q and loses to A, sitting in the middle. It checks and calls at frequency, while betting belongs to the poles (A and Q). Betting medium hands remains the most common amateur leak.

t9-mop-q7.question: The methodological value of toy games in MOP is:
options: isolating one variable so the mechanism becomes visible
they are closer to luck than real hands
t9-mop-q7.explanation: Toy games keep one or two variables and simplify to solvability. Simplification is not distortion but development; extrapolation still requires checking the extra variables of real play.

t9-mop-q8.question: In the AKQ equilibrium, Q's bluff frequency f and K's calling frequency c satisfy:
t9-mop-q8.explanation: Equilibrium requires f = B/(P+B) and c = P/(P+B), complements summing to 1. At pot size f=c=1/2; at one-third pot f=1/4 and c=3/4.

t9-icm-q6.question: Chip value diminishes at the margin in tournaments because:
options: prizes are paid in finish-order steps, so doubling chips does not double prize EV
t9-icm-q6.explanation: The prize structure is nonlinear: moving from third to second is worth far more than a chip double's probability gain. ICM converts that nonlinearity into finish probabilities and prize EV.

t9-icm-q7.question: A 55% shove can be positive cEV but negative $EV on the bubble because:
options: the finish-position loss when losing far exceeds the gain when winning
t9-icm-q7.explanation: Losing on the bubble zeroes prize EV, while winning chips adds only a limited prize gain. The same hand calls in cash and folds in a tournament because utility is nonlinear.

t9-icm-q8.question: Which stack faces the greatest ICM pressure?
options: a medium stack covered by a big stack
t9-icm-q8.explanation: A medium stack lacks the big stack's leverage yet fears elimination more than a short stack, making it the most likely to fold on the bubble. Big stacks pressure and short stacks must gamble.

t9-multiway-q6.question: AA against three random opponents wins about:
t9-multiway-q6.explanation: AA is about 85% against one, 73% against two and 64% against three. Each extra opponent dilutes equity and raises the made-hand threshold.

t9-multiway-q7.question: In multiway pots, bluff frequency should:
t9-multiway-q7.explanation: A bluff needs everyone to fold, and the all-fold rate falls exponentially with each player; each extra opponent is another chance to connect. Value multiway, pressure heads-up.

t9-multiway-q8.question: When re-ranking hands for multiway pots, prioritize:
t9-multiway-q8.explanation: Multiway pots raise the made-hand threshold, increasing the value of nut-making hands such as suited connectors and small pairs while dominating weak top pairs lose value.

t9-alpha-q6.question: For a 1.5x pot bet, Alpha is:
t9-alpha-q6.explanation: Alpha = 1.5 ÷ 2.5 = 60%, with MDF 40% as its complement; 37.5% is the caller's required equity.

t9-alpha-q7.question: The relationship between Alpha and MDF is:
t9-alpha-q7.explanation: MDF + Alpha = P/(P+B) + B/(P+B) = 1. At any size the fold rate the aggressor needs and the continue rate the defender must supply are exact complements.

t9-alpha-q8.question: Why is Alpha the wrong basis for saying the opponent bluffs enough to call?
options: Alpha is unrelated to the pot
Alpha is an aggressor metric for break-even bluffs, not a caller's standard
t9-alpha-q8.explanation: Alpha answers how much fold rate a bluff at this size needs; calling decisions use pot odds and the opponent's bluff share. Using an aggressor metric for defense is the classic misuse.

t9-unified-q6.question: The unified GTO-exploit framework writes a decision as:
options: equilibrium baseline + f(information quality) × targeted deviation
t9-unified-q6.explanation: The equilibrium baseline resists counter-exploitation while the size of the targeted deviation is set by sample quality. They are two modes of one system, not rival schools.

t9-unified-q7.question: The size of a deviation from equilibrium should be set by:
options: observation sample quality and the opponent's adaptability
t9-unified-q7.explanation: Without enough samples a deviation may be noise, and against an adaptive opponent a large deviation gets countered. Size scales with information quality and inversely with adaptability.

t9-unified-q8.question: How do the nine levels of theory ultimately create value?
options: being executed: repeating the correct process at the table
t9-unified-q8.explanation: Knowing MDF yet over-folding under pressure, understanding variance yet tilting anyway: the gap between knowing and doing is your ceiling. Theory has value only when executed.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q6.question: In cash, a 55% shove risking and winning 3000 chips has an expected result of:
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q6.explanation: 0.55×3000 − 0.45×3000 = +300 chips. Cash utility is linear, so positive expectation calls; the same hand may fold on a tournament bubble because $EV is negative.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q7.question: With 10000 chips and a 200 big blind, M=50. After blinds rise to 1000, M becomes:
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q7.explanation: M = effective stack ÷ big blind. Five times the blinds cuts M to one fifth: 50 → 10. Tournament depth collapses one way, removing postflop sizing families.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q8.question: Entry fees charged per buy-in versus rake charged per pot punish which behaviors?
options: fees punish volume, rake punishes entries
fees punish entries, rake punishes volume
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q8.explanation: Rake takes a share of every pot, punishing volume; an entry fee is charged per buy-in, punishing the number of entries. The forms differ and must be converted before comparing.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q9.question: When comparing cash and tournament returns, the right method is:
options: convert to the same time unit and risk basis
look at the top prize only
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q9.explanation: Cash is bb/100 × hands with linear utility; tournaments are per-event finish distributions with concentrated top payouts. Comparing raw amounts is comparing kilometers to kilograms.

t9-cash-vs-mtt-q10.question: The same 55% hand calls in cash but folds on the bubble because:
options: two ledgers: linear utility versus nonlinear prize utility
opponents have stronger hands on the bubble
t9-cash-vs-mtt-q10.explanation: The disagreement is not about skill but about which ledger is open: cEV in cash, $EV in tournaments. Confirm the ledger before every decision.

t9-sixmax-capstone-q4.question: The first step of the five-step decision chain is:
t9-sixmax-capstone-q4.explanation: Position and depth set the available streets, range width and commitment threshold, the coordinates for every later judgment. Skipping this removes the basis for all conclusions.

t9-sixmax-capstone-q5.question: Board ownership (range and nut advantage) primarily determines:
options: this street's betting frequency and sizing ceiling
t9-sixmax-capstone-q5.explanation: Range advantage decides whether you can bet often and nut advantage whether you can bet big. Ask whose board it is before assigning your hand a role.

t9-sixmax-capstone-q6.question: The main purpose of the leak self-check list is to:
options: locate repeated systematic errors and pick an exploit direction
t9-sixmax-capstone-q6.explanation: Long-term profit comes from repeating one decision chain. A self-check list finds the recurring error class, changing results more than memorizing any chart.

t9-sixmax-capstone-q7.question: Against a loose-passive pool that calls too much, the default exploit is:
options: widen value bets and bluff less
t9-sixmax-capstone-q7.explanation: Pool tendencies are the most stable exploit source. A loose-passive pool folds too little, so value bets earn more and bluffs lose, calling for wider value and fewer bluffs.

t9-sixmax-capstone-q8.question: The main source of long-term 6-max cash profit is:
t9-sixmax-capstone-q8.explanation: Long-term profit comes from process consistency, not highlights. Fixing a reviewable decision chain and correcting it with a self-check list beats any single trick.
